title: As If It Were the Sovereign
_note: Panama Canal pilot, screenplay v2, written 8 Nov 2026 by Fable from the Opus analyst's round-2 brief (reports/briefs/panama-pilot/fable-screenplay-brief.md). Nothing rendered, nothing downloaded. Voice durations are estimates (readings 3.0 w/s, narration 2.7 w/s); the engine measures the WAVs and the builders refit the times. Shots marked placeholder (the title slot, the v12 table shots, the typeset pages) are filled by the title builder and the drawn-pages unit; their ledger items state what they rest on and nothing more. The clip spans are provisional until the reels are viewed (A33). See screenplay-notes.md.

film_notes.text: Ten readings are heard in the translations their sources printed: Amador's address and Obaldía's, Valdés's, Herrán's and Reyes's notes in the State Department's Foreign Relations of the United States; Lesseps's Recollections in C. B. Pitman's English of 1887; Lesseps's circular of 9 February 1889 as the New-York Tribune printed it. Each is read in English because the extract is itself a translation.

The texts from the American Journal of Nursing (1905 and 1907) are relied on as public domain by date of publication; the JSTOR scan's non-commercial note is a condition of that copy, not of the text.
film_notes.source: open question 6; founder default of 8 Nov 2026

film_notes.text: The reel of President Taft's inspection (NARA 111-M-331, Record Group 111) is treated as a United States government work on the founder's default; the catalogue's use restriction read 'Undetermined' on 8 November 2026, and the reel's own intertitles credit the Feature Film Mfg. Co., Washington, D.C. Its catalogue date of 1910 is impossible (the Arkansas was commissioned in September 1912); the Canal Record has the President reach Cristobal on the Arkansas on 24 December 1912 and sail on the 26th.

Philippe Bunau-Varilla is placed with the French company, whose engineer he was in the years he writes of; in November 1903 he signed the canal convention for Panama. The founder is asked to confirm the side.
The flight that made the aerial reel was on 25 or 27 April 1913; the narration says April 1913 and does not choose a day.
The sick-pay rule card is dated by the report it quotes, the Canal Record of 1 July 1914; the month of the report is to be confirmed on the page image.

shots.why: Chapter card.

PLACEHOLDER table opener: the Muret relief panorama of the canal (LoC 2011590001) on the v12 table, the sea-level line in pencil; the title builder renders it. Under it, the first fact of the French attempt.
The title page of Lesseps's Recollections, read as a page, introducing the speaker without describing the frame.
The French cut at Bas Obispo in 1888 under Lesseps's own words of 1885 (A8 rule 3: the same place and period): the lock refused, then the promise of 1889 (M3, M4).

The sea-level canal near Tabernilla, photographed in 1911 with its caption's own 'Abandoned in 1888', under the second promise of 1889 (A8 rule 3, same subject; the mark carries 1911). Selection, nothing said (M3).
The woodcut of the French village at Aspinwall in 1885, the place and year of Bunau-Varilla's words (A8 rule 3).
The Tribune's front page of 10 February 1889 that printed the letter by cable, read as a page under the letter itself (A8 rule 5 with the real scan).
An old French ladder dredge at La Boca, photographed in 1907: the plant left standing, under the date work stopped.

text: “The commissioner sent by the Jamaican government has already sent away 4,000 people, and he has issued 3,000 tickets more, and these will leave by earliest steamers.”
shots.why: The Jamaican commissioner's 4,000 sent home, in the dispatch's own words, voiceless (M11; the answer comes in chapter 5 with the Ancon's 1,500).
Gatun station as it stood in the French period, under the New Company's date.
The French company's own lock profile of 1890, held with no voice: the lock Lesseps refused, drawn by his company a year after the failure (M4). The chapter ends on a frame.

lines.text: In December, eighteen eighty, the French canal company's stock was floated in Paris.
Ferdinand de Lesseps went to the Isthmus in eighteen eighty-six and wrote of his visit.

I intend to act just in the same way at Panama, though many engineers would prefer, on account of the difference in level, not of the seas, but of the tides, to construct a lock. I would not have one at Suez, and I do not intend to at Panama
lines.speaker: sp-lesseps

lines.text: These are the men who made the Suez and will make the Panama Canal, and Panama will be opened in 1889.
lines.speaker: sp-lesseps

lines.text: We saw whole mountains blown up with dynamite, blocks of stone measuring more than a hundred cubic yards sent up into the air like so many pebbles. We are delighted to be able to state, after the voyage which I have just made, that the canal will be open in 1889.
lines.speaker: sp-lesseps

lines.text: Philippe Bunau-Varilla, an engineer of the company at Colon in eighteen eighty-five, in a book of nineteen thirteen:

Meanwhile death was constantly gathering its harvest all about me. Never had the yellow fever been more deadly. Some fathoms only from my house at Colon, ships were anchored in the Company's harbour without a single soul on board. All the crew had died.
lines.speaker: sp-bunau-varilla

lines.text: On the fourth of February, eighteen eighty-nine, a liquidator was appointed. On the ninth, from Paris, Lesseps wrote to the shareholders.

I cannot, therefore, constitute a company for the completion of the Panama Canal. It will now be necessary to leave to the liquidator the care of our interests and the directing of a work which must yet be completed. We will show our confidence by calmly awaiting the decision of the liquidator.
lines.speaker: sp-lesseps

lines.text: Work was suspended on the fifteenth of May.
In October, eighteen ninety-four, a New Panama Canal Company was organised in Paris.

shots.why: Chapter card.
PLACEHOLDER table opener: the FRUS 1903 telegram pages (d229, d259, d280) on the v12 table; the page images are still to be located (brief, section 11). Under it, the Walker Commission's choice.

Colon in 1903, the year of the cables: dwellings of the old French company. The narration gives the dates; the cables follow as the period's own words. Framing: a stereograph card, shown whole by the engine's camera (a single-view framing is a founder item).

text: “Maintain free and uninterrupted transit. If interruption threatened by armed force, occupy the line of railroad. Prevent landing of any armed force with hostile intent, either Government or insurgent, either at Colon, Porto Bello, or other point.”
Navy Department to the USS Nashville, 2 November 1903
shots.why: The Navy's order of 2 November, voiceless, in date order with the two cables after it (M8: 'no shot', from three sides).

text: “Uprising occurred to-night, 6; no bloodshed. Army and navy officials taken prisoners. Government will be organized to-night, consisting three consuls, also cabinet.”
Felix Ehrman, United States vice-consul general, Panama, 3 November 1903
shots.why: Ehrman's 'no bloodshed' of 3 November, voiceless (M8).

text: “We take the liberty of bringing to the knowledge of your Government that on yesterday afternoon, in consequence of a popular and spontaneous movement of the people of this city, the independence of the Isthmus was proclaimed”
J. A. Arango, Federico Boyd and Tomás Arias, Panama, 4 November 1903
shots.why: The Junta's telegram of 4 November with its three signers, Federico Boyd among them (M2: he returns on the Land Commission in chapter 6); voiceless.
The Convention's own Article III page, read as a page while the narrator states the grant in its words (M9: inside and outside the Zone begins here).
A government's statement is read over a DRAWN typeset page of the document (A8 never-list); Herrán's protest, FRUS 1903 d273, typeset verbatim. PLACEHOLDER until the page is typeset.
Reyes's note of 23 December, its opening paragraph typeset as a page (A8 never-list). PLACEHOLDER.
The same note, p. 288, typeset: 'fought against no one' answers Ehrman's 'no bloodshed' and precedes Roosevelt's 'not a shot' (M8). PLACEHOLDER.
Roosevelt's annual message, p. XXXVI, typeset (A8 never-list: a government's statement over its own page). PLACEHOLDER.
Valdés's account, approved by the Junta, typeset from FRUS 1903 d328 (the State Department's translation; disclosed in the sources data, open question 12). PLACEHOLDER.

text: “The Government of the United States of America may intervene in any part of the Republic of Panama to restablish public peace and constitutional order in the event of their being disturbed”
Constitution of the Republic of Panama, Article 136, 1904
shots.why: Article 136 of the 1904 Constitution, voiceless: Panama's own text on intervention, before Obaldía's letter on sovereignty.

Women washing clothes at a spring near Panama City, 1904: the republic's own people in its first year, held with no voice (a rest, A10). Framing: a stereograph card, shown whole by the engine's camera (a single-view framing is a founder item).
Obaldía's letter of 11 August 1904 typeset as a page (A8 rule 5; no open-licence portrait is verified in the brief). The chapter's last reading is Panama's (M9). PLACEHOLDER.

lines.text: On the sixteenth of November, nineteen oh one, the Isthmian Canal Commission reported for the Panama route and a canal with locks.
On the second of November, nineteen oh three, the Navy Department cabled the gunboat Nashville, at Colon.
On the evening of the third, in the city of Panama, the independence of the Isthmus was proclaimed. About four hundred Colombian troops were at Colon.
On the eighteenth of November, at Washington, a convention was signed.

A zone ten miles wide, five miles on each side of the canal, the cities of Panama and Colon excepted, in which the United States would hold the rights it “would possess and exercise if it were the sovereign”.
Colombia protested: on the seventh of November through its chargé at Washington, Tomás Herrán,

I am discharging a duty by lodging in advance with your excellency, in the name of my Government, a solemn protest against the attitude assumed in the Department of Panama by the Government of the United States to the injury of Colombia's rights
lines.speaker: sp-herran

lines.text: and on the twenty-third of December through General Rafael Reyes.

The Government and people of Colombia consider themselves aggrieved by that of the United States in that they are convinced that the course followed by its administration, in relation to the events that have developed and recently been accomplished at Panama, have worked deep injury to their interests.
lines.speaker: sp-reyes

lines.text: The true character of the new State of Panama is revealed in the fact that it came into existence by a coup de main, effected by the winning over of troops, valorous without doubt, but who have fought against no one, assaulted no intrenchment, captured no fort
lines.speaker: sp-reyes

lines.text: Roosevelt, in his message to Congress of the seventh of December:

When it became evident that the treaty was hopelessly lost, the people of Panama rose literally as one man. Not a shot was fired by a single man on the Isthmus in the interest of the Colombian Government.
lines.speaker: sp-roosevelt

lines.text: In Panama, Ramón Valdés's account of the separation was approved by the Junta on the eighteenth of December.

the act executed on November 3 last is the logical sequence of a situation already unendurable, the solution of a grave and vexatious problem, the sincere, firm, definite, and irrevocable manifestation of the will of the people.
lines.speaker: sp-valdes

lines.text: On the eleventh of August, nineteen oh four, Obaldía, Panama's minister at Washington, to Secretary Hay:

Article III of the Varilla-Hay treaty, the only one treating of the rights of sovereignty, stipulates that the United States should (shall) possess and exercise the rights, power, and authority which the Republic of Panama conceded it over the zone, as if it were sovereign in the territory; but this expression implicitly conveys the idea that it is not sovereign
lines.speaker: sp-obaldia

shots.why: Chapter card.
December 1904, the month of Taft's banquet: an American steam shovel loading French dump cars, under the date of the visit.

sound.reason: a silent film; the Library of Congress file carries no original track

The mounted escort of the procession in the street (source 66.58 to 82.38 s, ending on its cut before the reel's damaged frames at 82.4 to 89.3 s) under the date; the Library of Congress's own head titles (0 to 13 s) are never shown. sound.reason: a silent film; the Library of Congress file carries no original track

The Library of Congress's head title on this file reads 'November 1916', an error of the title card's (the catalogue and the picture are of 1906); it is never shown. Span set 2026-11-08 on the viewed reel and its measured cuts (python -m studio.engine.clips bounds).
Roosevelt on the Decauville train in the Cut, November 1906: his own occasion under his own words about the Jamaica laborers he questioned there (A8 rule 2).
The market at Empire, 1905, held with no voice: the Isthmus the visitors passed through. The chapter ends on a frame.

lines.text: In November, nineteen oh four, William H. Taft, Secretary of War, came to Panama; on the first of December the government gave a banquet for him.
The fifteenth of November, nineteen oh six. President Roosevelt was received in the city of Panama by President Amador.
President Amador's address of welcome:

that of the great Colossus of the North, with its immense riches, unlimited credit, its vast store of knowledge, and numerous elements that contribute to make it the only entity capable of successfully carrying on such a great enterprise, with the small and the youngest republic of America, owner of the land, which she gladly lends for the work
lines.speaker: sp-amador

lines.text: For the first time in the history of the United States it has become advisable for a President of the United States to step on territory not beneath the flag of the United States, and it is in the territory of Panama that this has occurred
lines.speaker: sp-roosevelt

lines.text: He stayed three days on the Isthmus, and spent the second of them in the Culebra Cut.
To Congress, the seventeenth of December:

I questioned many of these Jamaica laborers as to the conditions of their work and what, if any, changes they wished. I received many complaints from them, but as regards most of these complaints they themselves contradicted one another.
lines.speaker: sp-roosevelt

shots.why: Chapter card.
Gorgas and his office force; the narrator names his post, and the hospitals his department staffed with nurses (F61).

sound.reason: a silent film; the Library of Congress file carries no original track

shots.cut_reason: ends 2.0 s before the train shot's own cut at 39.04 s: the shot's length is R55 and its tail, and the ride goes on in the source; the Library of Congress head titles (0 to 13.04 s) are never shown
shots.why: Gorgas on film, under his own words on the French (A8 rule 1): his portrait (13.04 s) then the ride on the rear platform past the Colon line. Span set 2026-11-08 on the viewed reel and its measured cuts (python -m studio.engine.clips bounds).
The larvicide plant at Ancon, 1910, under Gorgas's 1907 count of whites and yellow fever (A8 rule 3, the same subject; M14 begins).
Ancon Hospital from Ancon Hill, 1910, under the nurse who worked in it (A8 rule 3: the same place and period).
The operating room at Colon Hospital, 1910, under Freeland's ward (A8 rule 3, the same subject).

text: “There have been so many erroneous and exaggerated statements made regarding the conditions in the hospitals of Panama and the status of the nurses employed there that we, the nurses of Ancon, feel it incumbent upon us to refute these charges”
The nursing staff of Ancon Hospital, American Journal of Nursing, September 1905
shots.why: The Ancon nurses' unsigned statement of 1905 as a voiceless quote card (an unsigned author is never cast, A3 refined).
Quarters for the laborers at Cristobal under Roosevelt's count of their deaths in October 1906: the words are about the men the caption names (A8).
Grass burned beside a ditch, June 1910, under the Commission's own death rates by colour for the two years the record gives (F52; M14). The narrator gives the counts and nothing else.

text: “the whites receive pay for 24 days per year while sick from disease, while the blacks do not.”
shots.why: The sick-pay rule in the Record's own words of July 1914, voiceless (M14), dated by its content's report month (open question: the issue date to confirm).
The Ancon Hospital ambulance, 1906, the place and year of Chatfield's rebuttal (A8 rule 3). The chapter's last reading is a woman of the gold roll, a different side from chapter 3's.

lines.text: William Crawford Gorgas, chief sanitary officer of the Canal Zone.
Trained nurses served only at the Colon and Ancon hospitals; Ancon had five hundred beds and sixty-one nurses.

I have no intention of criticising the French. If we had come down here twenty-four years ago, situated as they were, I am not sure that we could have done very much better. In the first place, no one knew at that time how malaria or yellow fever was conveyed from one person to another
lines.speaker: sp-gorgas

lines.text: Gorgas, in the Medical Record, the eighteenth of May, nineteen oh seven:

I know of no disease that causes the panic among the whites that yellow fever does. [...] With a nonimmune force four times as large, for we now have over 10,000 whites, if we include women and children, we have passed fifteen months with not a single case of yellow fever.
lines.speaker: sp-gorgas

lines.text: Isabelle Freeland, a nurse at Ancon, in June nineteen oh seven:

There has not been a case of yellow fever in the hospital for nearly a year; vessels from South American ports are quarantined. Many accidents happen on the railroad and in digging the canal. Malaria and pneumonia are the medical cases, the latter being fatal to white or black men.
lines.speaker: sp-freeland

lines.text: To give an example of one ward: ward 3, section A, is a surgical ward for colored men; it has twenty-six beds and two private rooms.
lines.speaker: sp-freeland

lines.text: Roosevelt, to Congress, December nineteen oh six:
In October, of the 19,000 negroes on the roll 86 died from disease; pneumonia being the most destructive disease, and malarial fever coming second.
lines.speaker: sp-roosevelt

lines.text: In the year to June, nineteen oh seven, the Commission recorded one hundred and twenty-three deaths among its white employees, and one thousand one hundred and fifty among its black employees. In the year to June, nineteen thirteen: ninety-four, and three hundred and eighty-nine.
Mary Chatfield, a stenographer for the Commission at Cristobal, in letters printed in nineteen oh eight:

That women are debarred from taking the examinations for the positions in offices on the Isthmus is most unjust and senseless. The Isthmian Canal Commission sends plenty of trained nurses here, whose chief duty is to take care of colored men when they are sick
lines.speaker: sp-chatfield
lines.year_basis: the passage answers a letter of 26 September 1906 and bears no date of its own; it is printed in Light on Dark Places at Panama (1908), so 1906 or later, printed 1908 (text verification, 8 Nov 2026)

lines: Light on Dark Places at Panama, 1908

shots.why: Chapter card.
PLACEHOLDER table opener: the first page of The Canal Record, 4 September 1907 (IA canalrecord1152isth), on the v12 table; the title builder renders it.

text: “hereafter there shall be no distinction between employees on the gold rolls and those on the silver rolls”
shots.why: 'No distinction' in the Record's first number, voiceless (M13: the masthead of 1913 answers it at the chapter's end).
Newly arrived laborers mustered at Gorgona, under the Commission's own counts of the force by roll and of the recruiting in the West Indies (F10, F43; M11).
The Ancon coming into Cristobal with 1,500 laborers from Barbados, 2 September 1909 (M1: the same ship makes the opening transit in the close; M11 answers chapter 1's card).

The 'new style' kitchen for the laborers near Gorgona under Chatfield's letter of 1906 on the men who were given no covered place to cook (A8 rule 3: the same subject, the words about the men the caption names).
A Commission mess hall and family quarters, 1911, under Boswell on the women of the gold roll (A8 rule 3, the same subject).
The crowd waiting for the pay car at Culebra, January 1908, the year of Williams's letter about his pay (A8 rule 3; the caption names no community).
A West Indian wedding party at Culebra, 1913, with no voice: the record's own picture of the people whose words it does not hold (gap G1 is stated in the sources data, A56).
D Street, Colon, 1907, under Wheat's 'foreign country' and her silver dollars (A8 rule 3: the same place and period; M9, M12).
A West Indian laborer's house at Golden Green under Wilson's count of the colored men on the rolls: the words are about the people the caption names (A8).
A gang of 150 men shifting track by hand, January 1912, under Wilson's trains and shovels, then the medal cast from French copper (F49; M10 ties chapter 1 to the card that follows).

text: “1. American citizens alone shall be eligible for medals”
shots.why: The medal rule in the Record's own words, voiceless (M10).

text: “whose names are on the gold roll”
shots.why: The 1913 masthead answers 'no distinction' (M13), voiceless.

Williams's own letter on its page of the Washington Bee, 20 June 1908, under his sentence about white foreigners: A8 rule 5 as R12's Tribune page applies it (the real page in place of a typeset one); rules 1 to 3 hold for no picture whose caption names no community (the Gallego camp it replaces names one community under a voice from another: the never-list). Reorder stated (M12): Williams's 1908 letter closes the chapter after Wheat (1909) and Wilson (1910) so the chapter's last reading is a Black American, a different side from chapter 4's, and the three rolls end on the line that was drawn.

lines.text: The Canal Record, the Commission's own weekly, first appeared on the fourth of September, nineteen oh seven.

On the thirtieth of April, nineteen oh eight, thirty-three thousand one hundred and ninety-three were at work: five thousand eight hundred and thirty-one on the gold roll, twenty-seven thousand three hundred and sixty-two on the silver roll.
By July, nineteen oh nine, twenty-seven thousand five hundred had been recruited in the West Indies, seventeen thousand nine hundred and forty-nine of them in Barbados.
On the second of September, nineteen oh nine, the steamer Ancon came into Cristobal with fifteen hundred laborers from Barbados.
Mary Chatfield, from Cristobal, the second of August, nineteen oh six:

They are not allowed to cook in their quarters for fear of fire and no covered place is provided for them in which to cook, so these poor men exist under difficulties. [...] They receive the splendid wage of 10 cents, U. S. currency, an hour.
lines.speaker: sp-chatfield

lines.text: Helen Varick Boswell came to the Isthmus in September, nineteen oh seven, to organise women's clubs. To the New York Tribune, on her return:

You see, it has been very monotonous for the women on the Isthmus. The men had their work, but the women had only their housekeeping, and the housekeeping there isn't the absorbing thing it is with us. It is more like housekeeping in a camp.
lines.speaker: sp-boswell

lines.text: Henry Williams, a blacksmith helper from Houston, to William H. Taft, the sixteenth of June, nineteen oh eight:

I have been working as blacksmith helper for nearly a year, and was paid in gold. For some unexplained cause I was informed that I would be assigned to the silver roll, which woud greatly reduce me in pay and deprive me of certain benefits that are accorded to white foreigners who don't, understand their duties assigned to them.
lines.speaker: sp-williams

lines.text: Rhodelle Wheat, of La Boca, in a letter printed in New Hampshire, December nineteen oh nine:
I am really living on United States territory, as the canal zone belongs to the American government, but when we step foot on Colon or Panama city, we are in a foreign country.
lines.speaker: sp-wheat

lines.text: I say gold, as all Panamian money is silver, and ten silver dollars would only equal five American dollars
lines.speaker: sp-wheat

lines.text: W. W. Wilson, barber on the Isthmus from nineteen oh seven to nineteen ten, in the St. Louis Advance, August nineteen ten:

The employes are divided into two classes, termed silver employes and gold employes. All Americans are gold, and all others are silver employes. On all divisions and the Panama relocation railroad there are about 30,000 colored men, from Jamaica, Barbadoes, Grenada and Trinidad.
lines.speaker: sp-wilson

lines.text: They have on the canal over 500 dirt trains, daily; all are fired by colored men. They have over 300 steam shovels, all fired by colored men.
lines.speaker: sp-wilson

shots.why: The Executive Order of 5 December 1912 as the Record printed it, read as a page with no voice after its date (M9: 'take possession of all such land').
The old village of Gatun and the Chagres, February 1907, under the clearing of the lake towns (F32, F55, F56).
The remains of Frijoles, January 1912, with no voice.

Gorgona's shops, the debris burning, 22 September 1913, under the Record's note on the old town's owners (F58).
Cucaracha, 2 February 1913, under the Central Division's totals of earth and explosive (F40; M5, M6).
Tracks taken up on the bottom of the Cut before the water, 4 September 1913, under the count of the largest force (F35).

The crowd at Gatun awaiting the tug Gatun, 26 September 1913, under the first lockage and the lake's own rise (F38, F37). The chapter ends on a frame; its last reading is Goethals's, the Commission's side.

This is met by providing every possible safety device, by building the locks in duplicate and by the installation of a system by which the vessels will be controlled by powerful electric machinery on the lock walls, thus avoiding mistakes on the part of the vessels' crew or engine-room staff

lines.text: December, nineteen twelve. President Taft reached Cristobal on the twenty-fourth, aboard the Arkansas.
On the fifth of December, President Taft had signed an Executive Order on the lands of the Canal Zone.

The Gorgona district was abolished by order of the second of September, nineteen twelve. The towns of the old railroad line between Gorgona and Gatun were cleared: Bohio, Frijoles, San Pablo, Tabernilla.
Gorgona was moved between March and June, nineteen thirteen: two hundred American families, six hundred bachelors, several hundred West Indians.
A Joint Land Commission, Federico Boyd, Roland Falkner, Samuel Lewis and Leo Rowe, made awards for houses in Gorgona and Cruces.
The former owners in the old town of Gorgona were refused free transport for the material of their houses.

Between May, nineteen oh four, and August, nineteen thirteen, the Central Division took one hundred and nine million cubic yards from its territory, with about thirty-eight million pounds of explosives.
On the twenty-sixth of March, nineteen thirteen, the force was at its largest: forty-four thousand seven hundred and thirty-three.
On the twenty-sixth of September the tug Gatun was lifted through the west flight of the Gatun locks.
Gatun Lake had stood at thirty-one feet on the first of July, nineteen twelve. The sluices were closed on the twenty-seventh of June, nineteen thirteen.

shots.why: Loading the dike's holes with dynamite, 8 October 1913, under the firing by telegraph from Washington (F16, F39; M5: Lesseps's dynamite, the Division's explosive, the dike).
Goethals, Hodges and Harding at the dike, 1 October 1913, with no voice.
'First water in the cut', October 1913, with no voice.

text: “Half an hour or more after the dike was broken, a cayuco, or native canoe, made the passage through, followed shortly by three launches.”
shots.why: The cayuco first through the opened Cut, in the Record's words, voiceless (M15: the Ancon follows ten months on).
The crane boat La Valley leaving Miraflores lower locks, 7 January 1914 (F17; closes round-1 gap 3).
The La Valley in Pedro Miguel lock, the same day, dissolved from the last (one subject, one class), with no voice.
The Santa Clara towed by locomotives in a filling lock, 18 June 1914, with no voice (M4: the lock built).
The Cristobal passing Gatun upper locks, 3 August 1914, with no voice.
The Ancon on Gatun Lake near Mamei, 15 August 1914, under her timetable's first hours (F18, F42; M1: the ship of 1909).
The Ancon passing the Cucaracha slide, 15 August 1914, under the timetable's noon (F42; M6).

Bain's photograph of the Ancon in the Gatun locks, 15 August 1914, under the end of her day and Garrison's cable, the words about this event (A8). The last three readings (Williams, Goethals, Garrison) are three sides.

PLACEHOLDER table close: the ICC map of the Canal Zone, 1909 (LoC 92685993), on the v12 table with the Ancon's timetable traced in pencil; the title builder renders it. The one question, asked from inside 1914 (A0), then about eight seconds of room with no voice.

lines.text: At two minutes past two on the afternoon of the tenth of October, nineteen thirteen, President Wilson, at Washington, pressed a telegraph key, and the Gamboa dike was fired.
On the seventh of January, nineteen fourteen, the crane boat Alexandre La Valley passed through the locks at Pedro Miguel and Miraflores: the first steam vessel through from ocean to ocean.

The fifteenth of August, nineteen fourteen. The steamer Ancon left Cristobal at ten minutes past seven, with about two hundred guests aboard, President Porras of Panama among them. Gatun, eight o'clock.
Gamboa, a quarter past eleven. Cucaracha, twenty past twelve. Pedro Miguel, four minutes to one.
Miraflores, from four minutes to two until twenty past three. The end of the channel, half past four.
That day the Secretary of War, Lindley Garrison, cabled Goethals at Culebra.
By the successful passage of vessels through the Canal the dream of the centuries has become a reality.

subtitle_source.en:
The Isthmus of Panama. April, nineteen
thirteen.

A moving-picture camera, carried in a
hydro-biplane from Balboa on the Pacific
to Cristobal on the Atlantic.

In December, eighteen eighty, the French
canal company's stock was floated in
Paris.

Ferdinand de Lesseps went to the Isthmus
in eighteen eighty-six and wrote of his
visit.

I intend to act just in the same way at
Panama, though many engineers would

[Ferdinand de Lesseps,
Panama Canal Company, 1886]

prefer, on account of the difference in
level, not of the seas, but of the tides,

to construct a lock. I would not have one
at Suez, and I do not intend to at Panama

These are the men who made the Suez and
will make the Panama Canal, and Panama
will be opened in 1889.

We saw whole mountains blown up with
dynamite, blocks of stone measuring more

than a hundred cubic yards sent up into
the air like so many pebbles. We are

delighted to be able to state, after the
voyage which I have just made, that the
canal will be open in 1889.

Philippe Bunau-Varilla, an engineer of the
company at Colon in eighteen eighty-five,
in a book of nineteen thirteen:

Meanwhile death was constantly gathering
its harvest all about me. Never had the

[Philippe Bunau-Varilla,
French canal company, Colon, 1913]

yellow fever been more deadly. Some
fathoms only from my house at Colon, ships

were anchored in the Company's harbour
without a single soul on board. All the
crew had died.

On the fourth of February, eighteen
eighty-nine, a liquidator was appointed.

On the ninth, from Paris, Lesseps wrote to
the shareholders.

I cannot, therefore, constitute a company
for the completion of the Panama Canal. It

will now be necessary to leave to the
liquidator the care of our interests and

the directing of a work which must yet be
completed. We will show our confidence by

calmly awaiting the decision of the
liquidator.

Work was suspended on the fifteenth of
May.

In October, eighteen ninety-four, a New
Panama Canal Company was organised in
Paris.

On the sixteenth of November, nineteen oh
one, the Isthmian Canal Commission

reported for the Panama route and a canal
with locks.

On the second of November, nineteen oh
three, the Navy Department cabled the
gunboat Nashville, at Colon.

On the evening of the third, in the city
of Panama, the independence of the Isthmus

was proclaimed. About four hundred
Colombian troops were at Colon.

On the eighteenth of November, at
Washington, a convention was signed.

A zone ten miles wide, five miles on each
side of the canal, the cities of Panama

and Colon excepted, in which the United
States would hold the rights it “would

possess and exercise if it were the
sovereign”.

Colombia protested: on the seventh of
November through its chargé at Washington,
Tomás Herrán,

I am discharging a duty by lodging in
advance with your excellency, in the name

[Tomás Herrán,
Colombian chargé, Washington, 1903]

of my Government, a solemn protest against
the attitude assumed in the Department of

Panama by the Government of the United
States to the injury of Colombia's rights

and on the twenty-third of December
through General Rafael Reyes.

The Government and people of Colombia
consider themselves aggrieved by that of

[Rafael Reyes,
Envoy of Colombia, Washington, 1903]

the United States in that they are
convinced that the course followed by its

administration, in relation to the events
that have developed and recently been

accomplished at Panama, have worked deep
injury to their interests.

The true character of the new State of
Panama is revealed in the fact that it

came into existence by a coup de main,
effected by the winning over of troops,

valorous without doubt, but who have
fought against no one, assaulted no
intrenchment, captured no fort

Roosevelt, in his message to Congress of
the seventh of December:

When it became evident that the treaty was
hopelessly lost, the people of Panama rose

[Theodore Roosevelt,
President of the United States, 1903]

literally as one man. Not a shot was fired
by a single man on the Isthmus in the
interest of the Colombian Government.

In Panama, Ramón Valdés's account of the
separation was approved by the Junta on
the eighteenth of December.

the act executed on November 3 last is the
logical sequence of a situation already

[Ramón M. Valdés,
Panama, approved by the Junta, 1903]

unendurable, the solution of a grave and
vexatious problem, the sincere, firm,

definite, and irrevocable manifestation of
the will of the people.

On the eleventh of August, nineteen oh
four, Obaldía, Panama's minister at
Washington, to Secretary Hay:

Article III of the Varilla-Hay treaty, the
only one treating of the rights of

[José Domingo de Obaldía,
Minister of Panama, Washington, 1904]

sovereignty, stipulates that the United
States should (shall) possess and exercise

the rights, power, and authority which the
Republic of Panama conceded it over the

zone, as if it were sovereign in the
territory; but this expression implicitly
conveys the idea that it is not sovereign

In November, nineteen oh four, William H.
Taft, Secretary of War, came to Panama; on

the first of December the government gave
a banquet for him.

The fifteenth of November, nineteen oh
six. President Roosevelt was received in
the city of Panama by President Amador.
President Amador's address of welcome:

that of the great Colossus of the North,
with its immense riches, unlimited credit,

[Manuel Amador Guerrero,
President of Panama, 1906]

its vast store of knowledge, and numerous
elements that contribute to make it the

only entity capable of successfully
carrying on such a great enterprise, with

the small and the youngest republic of
America, owner of the land, which she
gladly lends for the work

For the first time in the history of the
United States it has become advisable for

[Theodore Roosevelt,
President of the United States, 1906]

a President of the United States to step
on territory not beneath the flag of the

United States, and it is in the territory
of Panama that this has occurred

He stayed three days on the Isthmus, and
spent the second of them in the Culebra
Cut.
To Congress, the seventeenth of December:

I questioned many of these Jamaica
laborers as to the conditions of their

work and what, if any, changes they
wished. I received many complaints from

them, but as regards most of these
complaints they themselves contradicted
one another.

William Crawford Gorgas, chief sanitary
officer of the Canal Zone.

Trained nurses served only at the Colon
and Ancon hospitals; Ancon had five
hundred beds and sixty-one nurses.

I have no intention of criticising the
French. If we had come down here

[William C. Gorgas,
Chief Sanitary Officer, Canal Zone, 1905]

twenty-four years ago, situated as they
were, I am not sure that we could have

done very much better. In the first place,
no one knew at that time how malaria or

yellow fever was conveyed from one person
to another

Gorgas, in the Medical Record, the
eighteenth of May, nineteen oh seven:

I know of no disease that causes the panic
among the whites that yellow fever does.

... With a nonimmune force four times as
large, for we now have over 10,000 whites,

if we include women and children, we have
passed fifteen months with not a single
case of yellow fever.

Isabelle Freeland, a nurse at Ancon, in
June nineteen oh seven:

There has not been a case of yellow fever
in the hospital for nearly a year; vessels

[Isabelle Freeland,
Nurse, Ancon Hospital, 1907]

from South American ports are quarantined.
Many accidents happen on the railroad and

in digging the canal. Malaria and
pneumonia are the medical cases, the
latter being fatal to white or black men.

To give an example of one ward: ward 3,
section A, is a surgical ward for colored

men; it has twenty-six beds and two
private rooms.

Roosevelt, to Congress, December nineteen
oh six:

In October, of the 19,000 negroes on the
roll 86 died from disease; pneumonia being

[Theodore Roosevelt,
President of the United States, 1906]

the most destructive disease, and malarial
fever coming second.

In the year to June, nineteen oh seven,
the Commission recorded one hundred and

twenty-three deaths among its white
employees, and one thousand one hundred

and fifty among its black employees. In
the year to June, nineteen thirteen:

ninety-four, and three hundred and
eighty-nine.

Mary Chatfield, a stenographer for the
Commission at Cristobal, in letters
printed in nineteen oh eight:

That women are debarred from taking the
examinations for the positions in offices

[Mary A. Chatfield,
Light on Dark Places at Panama, 1908]

on the Isthmus is most unjust and
senseless. The Isthmian Canal Commission

sends plenty of trained nurses here, whose
chief duty is to take care of colored men
when they are sick

The Canal Record, the Commission's own
weekly, first appeared on the fourth of
September, nineteen oh seven.

On the thirtieth of April, nineteen oh
eight, thirty-three thousand one hundred

and ninety-three were at work: five
thousand eight hundred and thirty-one on

the gold roll, twenty-seven thousand three
hundred and sixty-two on the silver roll.

By July, nineteen oh nine, twenty-seven
thousand five hundred had been recruited

in the West Indies, seventeen thousand
nine hundred and forty-nine of them in
Barbados.

On the second of September, nineteen oh
nine, the steamer Ancon came into

Cristobal with fifteen hundred laborers
from Barbados.

Mary Chatfield, from Cristobal, the second
of August, nineteen oh six:

They are not allowed to cook in their
quarters for fear of fire and no covered

[Mary A. Chatfield,
Stenographer, Canal Commission, 1906]

place is provided for them in which to
cook, so these poor men exist under

difficulties. ... They receive the
splendid wage of 10 cents, U. S. currency,
an hour.

Helen Varick Boswell came to the Isthmus
in September, nineteen oh seven, to

organise women's clubs. To the New York
Tribune, on her return:

You see, it has been very monotonous for
the women on the Isthmus. The men had

[Helen Varick Boswell,
Women's clubs, Canal Zone, 1907]

their work, but the women had only their
housekeeping, and the housekeeping there

isn't the absorbing thing it is with us.
It is more like housekeeping in a camp.

Henry Williams, a blacksmith helper from
Houston, to William H. Taft, the sixteenth
of June, nineteen oh eight:

I have been working as blacksmith helper
for nearly a year, and was paid in gold.

[Henry Williams,
Blacksmith helper, Canal Zone, 1908]

For some unexplained cause I was informed
that I would be assigned to the silver

roll, which woud greatly reduce me in pay
and deprive me of certain benefits that

are accorded to white foreigners who
don't, understand their duties assigned to
them.

Rhodelle Wheat, of La Boca, in a letter
printed in New Hampshire, December
nineteen oh nine:

I am really living on United States
territory, as the canal zone belongs to

[Rhodelle Emery Young Wheat,
La Boca, Canal Zone, 1909]

the American government, but when we step
foot on Colon or Panama city, we are in a
foreign country.

I say gold, as all Panamian money is
silver, and ten silver dollars would only
equal five American dollars

W. W. Wilson, barber on the Isthmus from
nineteen oh seven to nineteen ten, in the
St. Louis Advance, August nineteen ten:

The employes are divided into two classes,
termed silver employes and gold employes.

[W. W. Wilson,
Barber, on the Isthmus 1907 to 1910, 1910]

All Americans are gold, and all others are
silver employes. On all divisions and the

Panama relocation railroad there are about
30,000 colored men, from Jamaica,
Barbadoes, Grenada and Trinidad.

They have on the canal over 500 dirt
trains, daily; all are fired by colored

men. They have over 300 steam shovels, all
fired by colored men.

A medal for two years' service was cast
from the copper of old French excavators
and locomotives.

The moment a white foreigner arrives, who
does not know a word of English, he is
assigned to the gold roll.

In the winter of nineteen oh eight, one
hundred and three steam shovels in the Cut

moved more than two and a third million
cubic yards a month.

Goethals, in nineteen oh nine, on the
locks:

This is met by providing every possible
safety device, by building the locks in

[George W. Goethals,
Chairman, Isthmian Canal Commission, 1909]

duplicate and by the installation of a
system by which the vessels will be

controlled by powerful electric machinery
on the lock walls, thus avoiding mistakes

on the part of the vessels' crew or
engine-room staff

December, nineteen twelve. President Taft
reached Cristobal on the twenty-fourth,
aboard the Arkansas.

On the fifth of December, President Taft
had signed an Executive Order on the lands
of the Canal Zone.

The Gorgona district was abolished by
order of the second of September, nineteen

twelve. The towns of the old railroad line
between Gorgona and Gatun were cleared:
Bohio, Frijoles, San Pablo, Tabernilla.

Gorgona was moved between March and June,
nineteen thirteen: two hundred American

families, six hundred bachelors, several
hundred West Indians.

A Joint Land Commission, Federico Boyd,
Roland Falkner, Samuel Lewis and Leo Rowe,

made awards for houses in Gorgona and
Cruces.

The former owners in the old town of
Gorgona were refused free transport for
the material of their houses.

Between May, nineteen oh four, and August,
nineteen thirteen, the Central Division

took one hundred and nine million cubic
yards from its territory, with about
thirty-eight million pounds of explosives.

On the twenty-sixth of March, nineteen
thirteen, the force was at its largest:

forty-four thousand seven hundred and
thirty-three.

On the twenty-sixth of September the tug
Gatun was lifted through the west flight
of the Gatun locks.

Gatun Lake had stood at thirty-one feet on
the first of July, nineteen twelve. The

sluices were closed on the twenty-seventh
of June, nineteen thirteen.

At two minutes past two on the afternoon
of the tenth of October, nineteen

thirteen, President Wilson, at Washington,
pressed a telegraph key, and the Gamboa
dike was fired.

On the seventh of January, nineteen
fourteen, the crane boat Alexandre La

Valley passed through the locks at Pedro
Miguel and Miraflores: the first steam
vessel through from ocean to ocean.

The fifteenth of August, nineteen
fourteen. The steamer Ancon left Cristobal

at ten minutes past seven, with about two
hundred guests aboard, President Porras of
Panama among them. Gatun, eight o'clock.

Gamboa, a quarter past eleven. Cucaracha,
twenty past twelve. Pedro Miguel, four
minutes to one.

Miraflores, from four minutes to two until
twenty past three. The end of the channel,
half past four.

That day the Secretary of War, Lindley
Garrison, cabled Goethals at Culebra.

By the successful passage of vessels
through the Canal the dream of the

[Lindley M. Garrison,
Secretary of War, 1914]
centuries has become a reality.

When the water runs from one sea to the
other, whose ground is it running through?
